report.source_text: The CT scan revealed an irregular filling defect in the distal descending thoracic aorta, measuring 56×18×2 cm. Additionally, a 1.5 cm nodular filling defect was noted in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), with distal recanalisation and a subcapsular splenic infarction measuring 35×16 mm (figure 1). Given the presence of extensive and significant aortic atherosclerotic disease, these findings were initially interpreted as atherosclerotic thrombi. Notably, there was no evidence of thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysms, signs of intestinal ischaemia, gastrointestinal lesions suggestive of malignancy, abdominal lymphadenopathy or hepatic space-occupying lesions.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 80-year-old man with a history of smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral arterial disease presented with a 3-month history of constitutional symptoms including 8 kg unintentional weight loss and progressive anorexia, accompanied by abdominal discomfort and persistent constipation. Laboratory evaluation revealed iron-deficiency anemia (Hb 120 g/L, a 20 g/L decrease from baseline) and positive fecal occult blood testing (2/3 samples). Physical examination showed abdominal tenderness without peritonitis. CT angiography revealed an irregular filling defect in the distal descending thoracic aorta measuring 56×18×2 cm, initially interpreted as atherosclerotic thrombi, along with a 1.5 cm nodular filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery with distal recanalisation and a 35×16 mm subcapsular splenic infarction. Follow-up CT angiography 10 days later showed no interval changes. PET-CT imaging demonstrated a polylobulated, septated, hypodense lesion within the descending thoracic aorta and at the origin of the SMA with no significant radiotracer uptake and low suspicion for high-grade malignancy. The patient underwent open mesenteric thrombectomy within 24 hours with heparin infusion. In the immediate postoperative period, he developed acute arterial ischemia in both lower limbs requiring urgent bilateral transpopliteal thrombectomy. During this procedure, whitish and gelatinous embolic material was retrieved and sent for histopathological analysis. The patient's condition deteriorated rapidly with persistent hemodynamic instability despite high-dose vasoactive support, oliguria, and multiorgan failure due to massive embolic release.
